Findings.Comment: `totalWithVat` converts the cent-based subtotal into floating-point euros (`subtotal(lines) / 100`), multiplies by `(1 + vatRate)`, then converts back to cents. The project's blocking rule B1 requires money to stay integer cents (`Cents`) end to end and forbids arithmetic on amounts as floating-point euros, so this function violates it on every call. Findings.Comment: `Deliver`'s retry decision is inverted relative to the removed `if !retryable(err) { return err }` and to its own doc comment, which promises a transient failure is retried and a permanent one returned at once. `retryable` is `!errors.Is(err, ErrPermanent)`, so a transient 502 from the endpoint is returned on attempt 1 with no retry at all, while a permanent rejection (e.g. a 410 wrapped in `ErrPermanent`) falls through into the loop, logs "notification delivery failed, will retry", sleeps up to `maxBackoff`, and is pointlessly re-posted 5 times before being reported as "giving up after 5 attempts". Restore the negation so only transient errors go through the backoff loop.

Findings.Comment: The `defer resp.Body.Close()` guarding `resp, err := c.http.Do(req)` was removed, so `WhoAmI` never releases the response body it owns. Per the `net/http` contract the caller of `Do` must close the body, and `WhoAmI` returns only `*User`, so no caller can do it. On every call — including the non-2xx early return and the decode-error return — the underlying connection is never returned to the pool; under steady traffic this leaks file descriptors and idle connections until requests start failing.
Findings.Headline: WhoAmI no longer closes the HTTP response body

Expected.why: The response body is never closed on any path, so the underlying connection is leaked on every call, successful or not.

Findings.Comment: `Client.WhoAmI` no longer closes the response body it gets from `c.http.Do(req)`: the removed `defer resp.Body.Close()` was the only close in the function, and the full file contains no other `Close` call. Every call therefore leaks the body's file descriptor and keeps the underlying TCP connection checked out (Go cannot reuse the connection until the body is closed), so a caller that resolves the token owner repeatedly — e.g. once per incoming request — will exhaust connections or hit 'too many open files'. The error paths (`status %d` and `decode`) leak identically.

Any caller that invokes `WhoAmI` repeatedly (e.g. resolving the token's account per request) accumulates unclosed bodies: the underlying connection is never returned to the keep-alive pool and the process leaks file descriptors until dialing starts failing.

Findings.Comment: The two error-wrapping branches in `Owner` are swapped relative to the documented contract: `ErrNoClaim` is defined as what "callers match on when a project has no owner yet", and the comment says callers distinguish "nobody owns it" from a database fault with `errors.Is`. After this change, a missing row returns a wrapped `errNoRows` while a genuine database fault returns a wrapped `ErrNoClaim`. A caller that treats `errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim)` as "project is unclaimed" will therefore misclassify an outage as an empty claim table (and take over/claim a project), while real "no owner" results fall through to the fault path and surface as errors.
Findings.Headline: Owner() swaps ErrNoClaim and driver error wrapping

Expected.why: The branches wrap each other's error: errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim) is now false when the project is genuinely unclaimed and true when the query failed, so a database fault is treated as an unowned project.

Findings.Comment: This swap inverts the sentinel contract documented on `ErrNoClaim` ("what callers match on when a project has no owner yet"). Now the `errors.Is(err, errNoRows)` branch — the genuine "nobody owns it" case — returns the wrapped driver error, so a caller doing `errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim)` fails to detect an unowned project; conversely a real database fault returns `ErrNoClaim`, so a caller that falls back to claiming the project on that sentinel will treat a broken database as "no owner". The two `%w` operands need to be swapped back so `ErrNoClaim` wraps the no-rows case and `err` wraps everything else.

Findings.Comment: The two error returns are now swapped relative to the documented contract. On the realistic path where the project simply has no owner, `Scan` fails with `errNoRows`, and this branch now wraps that raw driver error instead of `ErrNoClaim`, so any caller doing `errors.Is(err, store.ErrNoClaim)` to distinguish "nobody owns it" will never match and will treat a normal empty result as a fault. Conversely, the `if err != nil` branch wraps `ErrNoClaim` for genuine database faults (connection loss, syntax error), so callers will treat an outage as "no owner" and may let an unowned project be claimed or silently drop data. The comment above `ErrNoClaim` and the function doc both state the opposite mapping.

As the function's own doc comment states, callers distinguish "nobody owns it" from a database fault with `errors.Is(err, ErrNoClaim)`.
